Thai computer teacher trainees must assemble and repair computers during their practicum, yet many get little hands-on practice because laboratory machines are scarce, outdated, and easily damaged. This design-and-development study built a virtual reality learning environment (VRLE) for computer assembly on a Meta Quest 3 headset, with controller-free hand tracking, three simulation rooms mapped to a national occupational competency unit, and learning media produced with generative AI. Development followed the ADDIE model, and a feasibility tryout used a one-group pretest–posttest design. Three content experts and three technical experts rated content (M = 4.74) and technical quality (M = 4.45) as very good, with interaction and usability the weakest domain (M = 4.11). Among 35 pre-service teachers with matched tests, achievement rose from 8.20 to 9.09 out of 10 (Wilcoxon z = 2.95, p = .002, r = .50; t(34) = 2.92, dz = 0.49). After a sequence of website lessons, VR practice, real-hardware practice, and debriefing, mean competency on real hardware was 4.85 (n = 36) and mean satisfaction was 4.79 (n = 28), both with ceiling effects. Without a control group, the results show that the VRLE is feasible and well received, not that it caused the gains.

Introduction This study examined changes in students' self-reported creativity-related behaviors following an educational intervention combining artificial intelligence (AI) tools and the DRAE instructional model (Diagnosis, Recreation, Application, and Estimation). Methods A one-group preexperimental pretest-posttest questionnaire design was complemented by semi-structured interviews and direct-observation records. The quantitative analysis included 551 valid paired EvaCreIA records, exceeding the minimum sample target of 543. The questionnaire assessed Generate Diverse Ideas (GID), Generate Creative Ideas (GIC), and Evaluate and Improve Ideas (EMI). Complementary interview indicators were calculated from 703 eligible pretest and 730 eligible posttest records, while direct observation included 568 completed checklist records. Results Posttest means exceeded pretest means by 0.222, 0.270, and 0.241 points for GID, GIC, and EMI, respectively, on a five-point scale. Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment ( p < .001). Rank-biserial correlations were 0.340 for GID, 0.387 for GIC, 0.340 for EMI, and 0.374 for the supplementary overall score. The complementary interview indicators showed higher favorable-response percentages at posttest. Discussion The results indicate changes in self-reported creativity-related behaviors following the combined educational intervention. However, retrospective record linkage, limitations in cross-instrument correspondence, self-report measurement, and the absence of a comparison group restrict causal interpretation. The findings do not establish an independent causal effect of AI or validate the DRAE model.

Although firms increasingly rely on social media to reach, high platform activity does not automatically yield user engagement and can suppress participation when communication strategies are misaligned. This underscores a central IS challenge: understanding how organizations can mobilize platform affordances to craft content that captures attention and stimulates interaction. Moreover, despite the importance of creativity for innovation and digital transformation, IS research has devoted limited attention to it, especially from a market perspective. As a result, we know relatively little about how organizational practices and managerial capabilities align with platform affordances to foster market-facing perceptions of creativity and, ultimately, customer-contributed value. Addressing these gaps, this study investigates how micro-level managerial capabilities and organizational routines relate to follower-perceived content creativity and multidimensional customer engagement. Utilizing multi-source, dyadic and triadic data from two empirical studies in Spain, we test a multilevel sociotechnical model using structural equation modeling. The findings indicate that organizational co-creation practices, as well as social media managers' task adaptivity and emotional intelligence, are positively associated with content originality and relevance through the enactment of platform affordances. Furthermore, follower-perceived content creativity is positively associated with second-order customer engagement, with market competitive intensity conditioning these pathways. The study advances affordance theory by extending its analytical scope from internal enterprise systems to open digital platforms, while conceptualizing digital creativity as an externally evaluated artifact. Practically, the results suggest that firms cannot rely on raw connectivity alone; managers and organizations must actively orchestrate adaptive iteration and collaborative listening to foster customer-contributed value.

Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.

The emergence of digital technologies, without doubt has continued to reshape educational systems across the globe, creating new opportunities for sustainable development in developing countries such as Nigeria. This study examines the nexus between emerging technologies and sustainable development with particular emphasis on digital learning systems in Nigeria. The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, virtual learning platforms, mobile technologies, and digital communication tools has significantly transformed teaching, learning and knowledge dissemination in educational institutions. Despite these advancements, challenges such as inadequate technological infrastructure, poor internet connectivity, digital inequality, limited technical skills and inconsistent policy implementation has continued to undermine the effectiveness of digital learning systems in Nigeria. The paper adopts qualitative approach and makes use of secondary sources of data to bridge the gap in knowledge. The study examines the role of emerging technologies in promoting sustainable digital learning systems in Nigeria, identify the challenges associated with the adoption of digital learning technologies in educational institutions; and investigate the challenges affecting the effective integration of emerging technologies into Nigeria's educational system. The paper hinges on the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovation Theory as its theoretical frameworks. While Technology Acceptance Model explains users' acceptance and utilization of digital technologies based on perceived usefulness and ease of use. The diffusion of Innovation Theory provides insight into how technological innovations spread are adopted within educational and social systems. The paper concludes that although emerging technologies possess significant potential for transforming Nigeria's educational landscape and advancing sustainable development, deliberate investments in infrastructure, digital literacy, and supportive policies are necessary for achieving long-term effectiveness and inclusiveness

Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled electrocardiography (ECG) can detect arrhythmias, structural abnormalities, and physiological patterns not readily apparent through conventional interpretation. However, its rapid clinical integration raises ethical concerns. This review critically synthesizes literature on bias and fairness, privacy and confidentiality, explainability and transparency, clinical trust and automation bias, and governance and accountability. Methods We conducted a narrative review using structured searches of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Review preparation was informed by the SANRA quality-assessment scale, and study selection was summarized using a flow diagram adapted from PRISMA-ScR (435 records identified; 46 studies included). Studies were eligible if they substantively examined ethical considerations in AI-ECG; those addressing technical performance alone were excluded. Evidence was classified by study design and clinical maturity. Results Ethical risks arose throughout the AI-ECG lifecycle, beyond the algorithm itself. Studies documented performance disparities across sex, age, race, and ethnicity, alongside vulnerabilities involving membership inference, biometric re-identification, and unintended attribute inference. Explainability remained inadequately evaluated, while automation bias raised concerns about clinical decision-making and patient safety. Governance and post-deployment oversight remained fragmented. Most quantitative evidence came from retrospective or experimental proof-of-concept studies rather than externally validated or clinically deployed systems. Discussion Responsible AI-ECG implementation requires a lifecycle approach addressing upstream bias, privacy safeguards, clinically meaningful explanations, clinician oversight, and post-deployment surveillance. We propose Inherent Protocol Bias (IPB) as an organizing framework linking downstream ethical risks to decisions in study design, data collection, validation, and deployment. Unlike dataset bias, selection bias, spectrum bias, measurement bias, and cohort-origin confounding, which describe specific sources or manifestations of error, IPB emphasizes the protocol-level decisions through which established biases arise or persist. IPB is not a new statistical form of bias but a framework for identifying actionable intervention points. We outline potential applications for improving fairness, privacy, accountability, and clinical trust; however, these recommendations remain conceptual and require empirical evaluation.

documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) offers opportunities to enhance students’ understanding but also raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty and the accuracy of religious information. This study aims to analyze AI use, teacher perceptions, students’ learning behaviors, and the ethical dilemmas arising at MA As Syakur. Employing a descriptive qualitative approach, the study involved one IRE teacher and eight Grade X students selected purposively. Data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of 33 student assignment books, then analyzed thematically. The findings reveal five patterns of AI use, ranging from seeking explanations and comparing information to directly copying AI-generated answers. Four of the eight student informants were found to have copied AI-generated answers into their assignment books. The teacher demonstrated an open yet cautious attitude, emphasizing the importance of guidance and information verification. This study highlights the need to promote AI literacy, academic honesty, and Islamic ethical values, particularly amanah (trustworthiness) and tabayyun (careful verification), in IRE learning. Future research should involve more madrasahs and employ longitudinal observations.

This primer discusses the ethical questions raised by computational social science (CSS), that is, research that analyses data generated at scale by digital platforms, networked devices, and public administrations. Much of the ethical guidance available to CSS researchers was developed for clinical and interventional research, and it assumes a bounded study, an identifiable participant, and an occasion on which consent can be sought. Since much CSS research lacks these features, the primer examines where this guidance fits and where it does not. The primer is organised around six themes: data, privacy, and power; bias and equity; conceptual clarity and value-laden choices; stakeholder impact, justice, and participatory research; ethical communication and public engagement; and the use of generative AI in the research process. Each theme is introduced conceptually, illustrated with cases from the published literature, and followed by reflection questions that researchers can ask of their own projects. The primer is intended for researchers, research ethics committees, and teaching. It pays particular attention to research on administrative registers, including data held by Statistics Netherlands. The research for this publication was partly funded by ODISSEI, the Dutch national research infrastructure for the social sciences.

documents.abstract: Exposure to hand transmitted vibration is common in workplaces using hand held-tools and contributes to upper limb disorders, including hand-arm vibration syndrome. Anti-vibration gloves are often the only personal protective equipment available, but their use remains limited because of discomfort and reduced manual dexterity, so glove assessment should extend beyond laboratory testing to real working conditions. This article proposes an extension of ISO 10819 based on eight vibration transmission coefficients determined in situ, together with comfort-related parameters such as dexterity and the force required to bend the fingers. The method was applied at four workstations differing in vibration characteristics, using an ISO 10819-compliant glove of a new design as a case study. Frequency-weighted exposure was reduced by 10-56% depending on the workstation, although at one workstation the results indicated amplification in one of the analysed axes. Compliance with ISO 10819 therefore does not guarantee protection at every workstation.

documents.abstract: Public companies increasingly communicate risks related to artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, automation, algorithmic decision-making, data privacy, security, bias, and regulatory uncertainty in annual risk-factor disclosures. However, assessing whether these AI-risk and trustworthy-AI communication claims are specific, evidence-grounded, or largely boilerplate remains difficult because Form 10-K Item 1A disclosures combine forward-looking risk language, legal disclaimers, product descriptions, governance statements, and uncertain regulatory developments. This study develops an evidence-grounded hybrid agentic AI framework for assessing AI risk communication in SEC Form 10-K disclosures. The task is framed as textual support assessment rather than an independent determination of a company's actual AI risk exposure, legal compliance, product safety, or trustworthiness. Using a corpus of 160 Form 10-K filings collected from SEC EDGAR, we identify 101 filings with AI-related Item 1A risk-factor language and construct an 80-claim manually annotated gold sample across 48 companies. We compare five approaches: a transparent rule-based baseline, a TF-IDF retrieval baseline, a single-prompt large language model (LLM) baseline, a pure multi-agent reasoning baseline, and the proposed hybrid agentic adjudication method. The hybrid method achieves the strongest performance on trustworthiness-dimension classification and evidence-support assessment, with 0.725 dimension accuracy, 0.667 dimension macro-F1, 0.750 support accuracy, and 0.734 support macro-F1. We further add an explainability and auditability analysis using claim-level audit traces and a SHAP-based structured-feature surrogate for supported versus non-supported evidence labels. The findings suggest that evidence-grounded hybrid agentic AI can support auditable analysis of trustworthy-AI risk communication, while also showing that direct LLM prompting can be poorly calibrated for evidence-support judgments.

This experimental study investigated how perceived workload is influenced by executive function load (lower, higher) and task engagement (via non-adaptive or adaptive task pacing), across the three domains of inhibition, switching, and updating. It further explored how mental fatigue develops from sustained performance under varying levels of these factors. Seventy-two adults were randomly allocated to three groups, each completing six tasks at an individualised pace and in a distinct combination of executive function load and task engagement. Workload was not altered by executive function load, but it increased significantly under adaptive pacing, with the most pronounced effect in the inhibition domain. Mental fatigue emerged across all conditions regardless of workload differences, but its onset was anticipated under low executive function load with non-adaptive pacing and under high executive function load with adaptive pacing. These findings suggest that under- and over-stimulation may be two different paths to mental fatigue.

Streaming Process Mining (SPM) enables the real-time analysis of business processes through the continuous processing of event streams, providing timely insights and facilitating quick decisions. Although SPM supports various applications in multiple domain areas, it often relies on data-driven algorithms that lack interpretability, limiting user acceptance and trust. To tackle such shortcomings, explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers promising techniques to improve transparency and understanding of the applied approach. Despite their complementarity, SPM and XAI originate from distinct research communities, each with its own focus, methodologies, and evaluation criteria. This paper provides an overview of the intersection between XAI and SPM. We categorize existing work according to the SPM tasks addressed, the XAI methodologies used, and the level of interpretability from the end-user’s perspective. In addition, we identify key research challenges and propose future directions aimed at developing more human-centered and trustworthy SPM approaches. Our findings emphasize the importance of aligning algorithmic performance and human comprehension to support responsible decision making in dynamic process environments.

documents.abstract: This study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) students demonstrate and develop Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) in generative AI-assisted essay revision. Drawing on the APSE model, which conceptualizes CAIL across four dimensions (awareness, positionality, interaction strategies, and evaluation), we conducted a longitudinal case study of three focal students across four writing tasks throughout a semester. Data sources included student-AI interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, stimulated recall interviews, and both initial and revised essay drafts. Qualitative analyses were conducted to trace patterns and changes in students’ CAIL. Findings show that all three students demonstrated CAIL across the four dimensions, although critical evaluation and critical positionality emerged as the most salient dimensions. Students selectively integrated AI feedback based on rhetorical fit, linguistic appropriateness, and factual accuracy, demonstrating various levels of agency. Over time, two students became increasingly selective and context-sensitive in their engagement with AI, whereas the third demonstrated strategic engagement from the outset but showed substantial task-to-task variation in feedback uptake. Overall, the students’ trajectories were heterogeneous and task-dependent rather than uniformly progressive. These patterns challenge linear models of AI literacy and highlight its situated nature in EFL writing contexts. Pedagogically, the study calls for differentiated instruction that fosters evaluative judgment and self-representation alongside prompt design. The findings contribute to a growing body of research advocating for more nuanced, learner-centered approaches to AI integration in foreign language writing.

Eye and face protection violations under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard have repeatedly appeared among the most frequently cited federal workplace safety standards since fiscal year 2018, highlighting persistent challenges in personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance, hazard recognition, and occupational safety management. Workers in construction, manufacturing, and other high-risk industrial environments remain vulnerable to eye and facial injuries arising from flying particles, chemical splashes, molten materials, dust, and other hazardous exposures. Although conventional workplace inspections, safety training, and supervisory monitoring remain essential, these approaches are often constrained by limited observation coverage, intermittent assessments, delayed identification of violations, and inconsistent enforcement. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and edge computing offer opportunities to strengthen PPE monitoring through automated recognition, contextual risk assessment, and timely corrective intervention. This study examines the regulatory, technological, and operational challenges associated with persistent eye and face protection violations and develops an evidence-based framework for integrating AI-assisted PPE detection with proactive occupational safety management. Specifically, it investigates how deep learning-based object detection, worker–PPE association, pose estimation, edge inference, hazard-aware decision rules, and human-centered intervention mechanisms can improve the identification, prioritization, and resolution of potentially unsafe PPE practices. An evidence-based narrative synthesis was conducted using OSHA regulatory information and peer-reviewed literature addressing occupational eye and face injuries, PPE compliance monitoring, computer vision architectures, machine learning, workplace hazard assessment, and safety management systems. Particular attention was given to You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detection models, pose and key point estimation, lightweight edge-computing architectures, temporal tracking, and multiclass PPE classification. Existing studies were critically examined to identify methodological strengths, operational limitations, performance variability, and research gaps. Building on the reviewed evidence, this study develops a risk-informed occupational eye and face protection assessment methodology that integrates regulatory requirements, hazard exposure, protective equipment adequacy, monitoring reliability, and corrective intervention effectiveness. Rather than proposing another automated PPE detection architecture, the methodology examines how technology-generated observations can be interpreted within task-specific safety requirements and translated into measurable intervention priorities. It distinguishes confirmed equipment absence, incorrect positioning, unsuitable protection, and insufficient visual evidence while incorporating mathematical indicators for hazard-weighted prioritization, detection reliability, corrective-action timeliness, and occupational injury incidence. Computer vision and edge-based monitoring are examined as supporting sources of safety evidence rather than independent injury-prevention solutions. The resulting methodology provides a structured basis for prospective evaluation of monitoring-supported safety interventions. No newly trained detection model, experimental dataset, or completed field trial is reported. Unlike conventional PPE recognition systems that primarily identify equipment presence, the framework emphasizes whether appropriate protective equipment is correctly positioned, associated with the exposed worker, and suitable for the prevailing occupational hazard. It also incorporates human oversight, privacy safeguards, explainable decision support, and mechanisms for managing false-positive detections and ambiguous visual conditions. The study proposes a multidimensional evaluation strategy extending beyond conventional computer vision metrics such as precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed. Recommended performance indicators include event-level violation detection sensitivity, false alerts per worker-hour, end-to-end notification latency, time to verified corrective action, unresolved hazardous exposure duration, recurrence of PPE violations, and longitudinal occupational injury outcomes. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for comparing AI-assisted monitoring with conventional safety inspection approaches while distinguishing technical detection performance from operational intervention effectiveness. It further identifies research priorities involving small-object recognition, transparent protective eyewear detection, cross-site generalizability, risk-based alert optimization, worker privacy, and prospective validation of injury-prevention outcomes. AI-assisted eye and face protection monitoring represents a promising approach to addressing persistent PPE compliance challenges through continuous observation, contextual violation assessment, and timely intervention. However, high detection accuracy and rapid alert generation alone do not demonstrate reductions in occupational injuries. Effective prevention requires reliable worker - PPE association, hazard-specific compliance assessment, accountable human intervention, verified corrective action, and integration with established occupational safety procedures. The proposed framework advances the conceptual foundation for transforming automated PPE recognition into a measurable, human-centered workplace safety intervention. Future empirical research should validate the framework across diverse industrial environments and determine whether improved violation detection and corrective-action timeliness translate into sustained reductions in hazardous exposure and preventable eye and face injuries.

Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.

documents.abstract: Hidden capture is a loss of skill that the people losing it do not notice, combined with a dependence that does not reverse when the pressure behind it eases. The Correction Freeze Problem predicts this pattern, but testing it on human thinking would take decades of data that do not yet exist for generative AI. We therefore built a computer simulation of a population, calibrated to what can be measured today, and followed it across generations in two worlds that share the same machines. In World M, AI mostly replaces people’s own practice, and each generation learns what normal ability looks like from the one before. In World N, AI mostly supports practice, and each generation’s sense of normal ability is anchored in direct experience, including time in nature. The model reproduces today’s rise of AI-written text in student work, the share of people who check AI output, and how loosely people’s opinions of their own thinking track tested performance. The simulations show what a captured world would be like from the inside. Delegation stays modest for a while and then sweeps through most of the population within a few years, because each person who hands over their thinking makes it more normal for everyone else. Skill then drains away without being felt. In World M, the average person’s unaided ability fell to about the bottom tenth of the population before AI, yet people registered only a small part of that loss, about a quarter even a century later, because their machine-assisted work looked as good as ever and everyone around them had declined too. The habit of checking disappeared first: at full delegation, only two people in a hundred still compared the machine’s answers with their own judgment, and when the machine’s error rate was quietly doubled, about one in a hundred noticed within five years. In an illustrative century, easing the pressure after a generation of heavy delegation restored only World N; the other two worlds were still captured half a century later. Staying out of the trap proved far easier than climbing out of it. These findings are conditional projections, not forecasts. Across 2,176 sensitivity runs, the unseen loss appeared every time, and its size depended mainly on two things societies can influence now: whether AI replaces or supports people’s own practice, and whether each generation anchors its sense of competence in direct experience. Whether capture can be undone depended on one quantity not yet measured, how much an individual’s reliance on AI changes from year to year; if reliance churns, capture becomes reversible, though it stays hidden. Several earlier results weakened as the model was corrected, and the main pre-specified test of a final extension came back negative; both are reported.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

documents.abstract: Large digitised media collections often remain unprocessed and unexplored, despite being technically preserved, and archival institutions increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI). Rather than pursuing autonomous archival systems, this article examines how AI can support archival description and classification while preserving the contextual, historical and provenance-related integrity of archival materials. Drawing on the archive of media artist Teoman Madra (1931–2025), the study develops and evaluates an AI-assisted archival tool for a large, initially unstructured collection. The proposed approach establishes an iterative, human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI-generated suggestions are critically assessed by the archivist, whose decisions subsequently inform the system's outputs. The study shows that the controlled vocabulary given to the model shapes what it can recognise, that the archivist's validated decisions guide classification reliably within an archival unit but not across units, and that the model's contribution declines as tasks demand contextual knowledge beyond what is visible. While this process can improve efficiency and reveal details a person might miss, it also introduces epistemic risks, particularly when plausible but inaccurate classifications remain undetected. Faster processing does not by itself mean more reliable description. The article conceptualises AI-assisted archival classification as archival affirmation, a collaborative process in which human judgement remains integral to the production and validation of archival knowledge. By situating the archivist's interpretive authority at the centre of this process, the article contributes to discussions of the responsible integration, critical oversight and governance of AI in archival practice.

Eliyas Kebede Zemedkun, in his treatise From the Age of Reason to the Age of Algorithm, critically examines human sociocultural and political evolution, tracing the shift from mythological bewilderment and the worship of Logos to empiricism and the ultimate apotheosis of the algorithm. The author shows how truth migrated from God and mind to machines, leaving humanity excluded from knowledge production to become mere receivers. This technological deity operates as both servant and master, subsuming divine and demonic traits under automated architectures.Addressing the post human predicament, Zemedkun argues that surrendering truth, justice, and religion to algorithms evacuates human agency. Surveillance capitalism shifts from physical labor exploitation to cognitive exploitation, harvesting human thoughts, language, and art to train artificial intelligence models. Through the automation paradox, artificial intelligence accelerates capitalist self destruction by displacing industrial labor and eviscerating public purchasing capacity. Applying Nietzschean philosophy and the master slave dialectic, the author warns that delegating thought kills the will to power, creating the Last Man and reducing future generations to prompting animals. Foucault disciplinary power, Marcuse one dimensional digital man, and Derrida textual deconstruction trap humanity in simulated reason, shifting the paradigm from I think therefore I am to I prompt therefore I am.To rescue the general will from digital anarchy, Zemedkun introduces the Information Contract as a reciprocal normative commitment among citizens and institutions to protect information integrity based on mutual veracity. Distinguishing state formation as hardware from nation building as software, the author emphasizes that sustainable nations require information integrity rather than foundations built on myths. Concluding that the cognitive will to truth is what has died, Zemedkun asserts that society must embrace the Information Contract to avoid collapsing into a digital Hobbesian state of nature.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is commonly used to generate answers, assist writing, and provide feedback. This article develops another educational role: the international critical peer for educators. In this role, educators use GenAI to surface assumptions and identify alternative interpretations when planning, designing, or making decisions across cultural and educational contexts. Drawing on work in global competence, intercultural competence, global citizenship education, and GenAI-supported critical feedback, this article presents a guided inquiry process for educators. The process begins with a real question, uses GenAI to surface possibilities, examines those possibilities through relevant evidence and input from people with experience in the setting, and then returns to the original decision. The aim is to expand professional inquiry while keeping interpretation and judgment with the educator.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.

documents.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

documents.abstract: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become routine in engineering classrooms, yet acceptance research treats use behaviour as the terminal outcome of adoption and cannot ask what it displaces. This study extends UTAUT2 with four education-specific constructs (academic integrity concern, AI trust, personal innovativeness, learning self-efficacy) and adds a second endogenous outcome absent from the acceptance canon: human-help displacement, the contraction in how often a respondent turns to another person for help, not a measure of help quality or learning impairment. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was applied to N = 392 engineering students and educators at Philippine higher-education institutions (n = 347 for the displacement model), complemented by necessary condition and multi-group analyses. Displacement was the best-explained construct (R 2 = 0.73) and was associated overwhelmingly with habit ( = 0.71), not intention (direct = 0.04, ns; the total association is small but non-zero), although intention was associated with use behaviour ( = 0.32; = 0.28). This path was negligible-to-small rather than null, and an ordered-logit specification reproduced the pattern. Academic integrity concern was the only factor inversely associated with displacement ( = 0.33). An exploratory necessary condition analysis showed a ceiling pattern consistent with habit acting as a threshold, and no corrected structural difference was detected between students and educators, though the educator subsample is underpowered to establish equivalence. Because habit and displacement were measured contemporaneously, causal direction cannot be established. The findings identify a correlate of adoption that intention-based models cannot see, and motivate habit-aware institutional intervention as a hypothesis for future evaluation.

documents.abstract: Choosing an AI model for business is not simply about picking the most popular platform or the model with the strongest benchmark score. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini can all support business teams, but they differ in how they handle reasoning, writing, multimodal tasks, integrations, and ecosystem compatibility. The best AI model for business is the one that fits your actual workflows, data requirements, and long-term AI strategy. What makes an AI model suitable for business? Different teams expect different things from AI. Some companies may need strong writing and analysis capabilities, while others may prioritize multimodal workflows, automation, internal knowledge support, or integration with existing tools. That is why an AI model comparison for business should focus on practical use cases rather than model popularity alone. Teams need to understand how each option performs in the environments where it will actually be used. Comparing Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are all capable AI platforms, but they are not interchangeable. Their strengths may differ depending on the type of work being performed and the ecosystem in which the company operates. For example, one model may be a better fit for long-form reasoning or content generation, while another may be stronger for multimodal tasks, integrations, or workflows connected to a particular technology stack. A useful comparison should therefore look at capabilities in the context of real business tasks. Choosing the right AI model Choosing the right AI model starts with understanding the problem you want AI to solve. Instead of adopting a platform because competitors are using it, businesses should identify the workflows where AI can provide measurable value. This may include internal knowledge support, content creation, research, data analysis, automation, or customer-facing tools. Once the use case is clear, teams can compare model capabilities, costs, integration options, and operational requirements more effectively. Enterprise considerations For larger organizations, the decision becomes more complex. An enterprise AI model comparison should consider not only performance, but also security, compliance, governance, scalability, integration requirements, and user adoption. The model may eventually become part of daily operations across several departments, which means long-term maintainability and compatibility with internal systems matter just as much as individual features. Final thoughts There is no single best AI model for business that works for every company. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini each offer different strengths, and the right choice depends on how AI will be used inside the organization. By focusing on real workflows, integration requirements, security expectations, scalability, and business goals, companies can make a more practical AI model comparison for business and choose a platform that supports both current needs and future AI adoption.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can already participate in literature retrieval, question generation, coding, analysis, interpretation, and manuscript production, making fixed task-based rules about what should remain human increasingly unstable. This conceptual article introduces a Counterfactual Boundary Test for distinguishing why human involvement is retained in AI-assisted research. The test asks whether the rationale for human involvement would disappear if the relevant AI limitation disappeared. If so, the ground is capability-contingent; if the rationale persists because the work continues to be substantively attributed to human authors, the ground is human-authorship-related; other ethical, legal, fiduciary, political, or social grounds may remain distinct. Current hallucination and verification risks illustrate the first case, whereas comprehension, critical evaluation, justified acceptance, and accountability provide a parsimonious diagnostic synthesis for examining the second. The framework does not claim that all future science must remain human. Instead, it clarifies which rationales may move with technological capability and which arise specifically under human-authored science. These indicators do not replace the cumulative International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) authorship criteria. A worked citation-validation example illustrates selective revision of controls, and a specialist-coauthor case explains justified reliance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can expand the resources available for primary mathematics teaching, but assisted task completion is not the same as mathematical learning. This article develops a Human-Centred AI Pedagogy Framework through a synthesis of sociocultural theory and humans-with-media, human-centred AI and hybrid intelligence, social cognitive theory, TPACK and its AI extensions, and Ubuntu-informed relational ethics. The framework connects pedagogical intentionality, teacher agency, learner agency, mathematical sense-making, and ethical and relational responsibility. Its proposed explanatory contribution concerns the destination of mathematical decisions in a teacher–child–AI relationship. When teachers reduce direct guidance, decisions may be delegated to children or taken over by the system; this paper describes the latter possibility as decision drift. Agency handover, therefore, means increasing children's supported responsibility for strategy, representation, justification, and help-seeking, while teachers retain safeguarding and instructional accountability. The dimensions are differentiated as prerequisites, enabling conditions, mediating processes, outcomes and ethical boundaries. Two hypothetical lessons, on Grade 3 place value and Grade 5 growing patterns, illustrate the framework and compare AI-supported and non-AI alternatives. South African multilingualism, unequal infrastructure and teacher workload specify important implementation conditions. Five propositions identify expected relationships, observable indicators and competing explanations, providing a basis for classroom observation and comparative studies. Evidence from older learners motivates the analysis but does not establish effects in primary classrooms. The framework's explanatory and predictive validity remains to be tested; its value is a more precise account of what AI-mediated mathematical activity should enable, protect and make open to investigation.

documents.abstract: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load (t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation (t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cybersecurity systems to support threat detection, security monitoring, incident analysis, and decision-making. The ability of AI systems to process large volumes of security information and provide rapid recommendations can improve the efficiency of cybersecurity operations. However, the increasing dependence on AI may also influence how humans evaluate security information and respond to potential threats. In particular, differences in AI reliability may affect user trust, confidence, independent verification, and vigilance during cybersecurity decision-making. This paper examines the relationship between AI reliability and human vigilance in AI-assisted cybersecurity decision loops, with particular attention to trust, decision accuracy, confidence, verification behaviour, and human judgement. Drawing on existing literature related to human-AI collaboration, automation bias, cybersecurity decision-making, trust in AI, and cognitive behaviour, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI reliability, human trust, cognitive vigilance, verification behaviour, and cybersecurity decision quality. The paper considers AI as a decision-support mechanism rather than a complete replacement for human judgement. While reliable AI recommendations may support faster and more effective decisions, inappropriate reliance on AI may reduce independent evaluation and increase the possibility of accepting incorrect recommendations. The proposed framework provides a basis for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI reliability influence human vigilance and decision-making in cybersecurity environments.

documents.abstract: Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming pedagogical practices in Cameroonian secondary education. This study assesses the influence of teachers' experience using GenAI tools on how secondary school teachers in Yaoundé perceive the reliability and compliance of generated content with the guidelines of the Competency-Based Approach (CBA). Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, 370 teachers were surveyed by questionnaire and 130 others through semi-structured interviews (total N = 500). The Chi-square test reveals a highly significant association between GenAI user status and the perception of the quality of generated content (χ 2 (3) = 41.527; p < 0.001; Cramer's V = 0.335). Among users, 33.46% described the content as "contextual" compared to 15.38% of non-users. The interviews explain this difference through the progressive learning of contextual prompt engineering. However, 65.9% of all respondents judged the generated lesson plans to be poorly compliant with CBA guidelines. The study concludes that while direct experience improves the perception of GenAI, the structural deficit in African contextualization of large language models remains a major obstacle, which only targeted prompt engineering training and the development of better-adapted tools will be able to overcome.

documents.abstract: Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

documents.abstract: This review systematically identifies and synthesizes implementation barriers reported in the literature regarding artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support systems in oncology. Following PRISMA guidelines, an initial search of the Scopus and PubMed databases and a subsequent citation-prioritized update identified review articles published between January 2021 and December 2025, of which 113 met the inclusion criteria. The review addresses five interconnected barriers: model interpretability, external validation, fairness and class imbalance, electronic health record integration, and data standardization. External validation is the most frequently cited challenge (73.5%), followed by model interpretability (66.4%) and data standardization (65.5%). Temporal trends show a marked increase in validation concerns, from 56.7% in 2021 to 93.8% in 2025, and declining attention to fairness barriers, from 53.3% in 2021 to 37.5% in 2025. This paper makes four main contributions. First, it presents an integrative framework showing that the barriers form an interconnected system in which fairness propagates into all downstream components, so that the observed decline in explicit fairness research signals a critical gap in current priorities. Second, it quantifies barrier prevalence and its temporal evolution, enabling evidence-based prioritization. Third, it consolidates the approaches reported in the literature into unified pipelines for bias mitigation and model interpretation. Fourth, it proposes a stage-specific implementation protocol with a decision flowchart to guide barrier assessment before deployment in screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis applications. The findings indicate that effective AI implementation in oncology requires addressing multiple barriers simultaneously rather than in isolation. The proposed frameworks and implementation protocol provide actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners working to translate AI models from development to clinical practice.

With machine learning, natural language processing and learning analytics, a platform can respond better to the different needs of its students. This paper looks at what AI can do in education and sets out a conceptual framework for an intelligent learning environment, one that combines learner information, adaptive materials, automated feedback and guidance from teachers. It covers personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, regular assessment, early identification of learning difficulties and accessibility. It also takes up the concerns that come with these tools: student privacy, bias, unequal access to technology, inaccurate AI-generated content, academic honesty and overdependence. The paper rests on a focused review of selected academic and policy literature. It reports no new experiment and no original student data. Its argument is that AI can make learning more supportive and flexible when used responsibly, and that it should assist teachers and students rather than replace the judgement, effort and human contact that education depends on.

This study explores the roles of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in influencing students' academic engagement and success at the State Islamic College of Mandailing Natal. A qualitative descriptive approach, utilizing interviews, observations, and document analysis, was employed to gain an in-depth understanding of how these motivational factors contribute to students' learning outcomes. The findings reveal that intrinsic motivation, driven by personal interest and curiosity, plays a more dominant role in sustaining long-term engagement and deeper learning. Students who were intrinsically motivated tended to show greater proactive involvement in their studies, going beyond formal requirements and seeking additional resources. However, extrinsic motivation, such as grades, praise, and career prospects, also played a significant role, particularly in initiating engagement and guiding academic goals, especially in structured academic settings. The study highlights the dynamic interaction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, demonstrating that both can coexist and complement each other. Additionally, contextual and instructional factors, including teaching methods, classroom atmosphere, and instructor support, were found to significantly impact students' motivational responses. The study concludes that fostering a balanced approach to motivation, combining both intrinsic and extrinsic elements, can enhance students' academic performance and long-term engagement with learning. Suggestions for educators include adopting interactive, student-centered teaching methods and creating a supportive learning environment that encourages both types of motivation to thrive

Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pharmacy education faster than curricula have adapted, yet evidence on how pharmacy students in sub-Saharan Africa understand and use it is almost absent. We assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) regarding AI among pharmacy students in a Francophone (Guinea) and an Anglophone (Malawi) country, and identified their determinants. Methods A multicentre online cross-sectional survey (29 March–12 June 2026) included pharmacy students from three universities in Conakry, Guinea, and from Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Malawi. A bilingual self-administered questionnaire measured knowledge (9 items), attitudes (8 Likert items) and practices (7 items, score 0–11). Prespecified cut-offs defined adequate knowledge (≥ 70%), favourable attitude (≥ 75%) and adequate practice (≥ 8/11). Multivariable logistic regression models, structured along the KAP pathway, estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 participants (Guinea 115, Malawi 207; median age 23 years), 99.7% had heard of AI and 96.2% had used AI tools, but only 27.9% had received formal AI training. Adequate knowledge was found in 32.0% (95% CI 27.1–37.3), favourable attitudes in 30.2% (25.4–35.4) and adequate practices in 64.3% (58.9–69.3). Half of the students (49.8%) believed that AI always provides correct results, and only 18.9% always verified AI-generated information. The two countries showed mirror-image profiles: Malawian students knew AI applications better and were more favourable to AI (aOR 3.77; 1.79–7.97), whereas Guinean students more often recognised AI's limitations and verified its outputs. Adequate practice was independently associated with adequate knowledge (aOR 2.28; 1.26–4.13) and favourable attitude (aOR 2.57; 1.40–4.73), and inversely with age > 23 years (aOR 0.39; 0.21–0.74) and studying in Malawi (aOR 0.39; 0.19–0.81). Advanced years of study predicted adequate knowledge (≥ 5th year: aOR 4.62; 1.27–16.87), while self-reported formal AI training was not associated with better knowledge. Conclusions Pharmacy students in both countries use AI almost universally but lack the critical knowledge needed to use it safely, with a high risk of automation bias. Curricula should move beyond tool familiarity towards structured, competency-based AI literacy centred on output verification, limitations, ethics and pharmacist accountability, adapted to each national context.
